power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Domestic Gender-Based Violence and Sexual and Reproductive Health-Seeking Behavior Among Women in Lusaaze Informal Settlement, Kampala, Uganda

text.text: Background: Domestic gender-based violence (DGBV) can undermine women's sexual and reproductive health (SRH) and reproductive autonomy.
However, community-level evidence examining multiple forms of violence and their relationship with SRH-seeking behaviour in Uganda's informal urban settlements remains limited.
This study assessed the prevalence of DGBV, associated factors and its relationship with SRH-seeking behaviour among women in Lusaaze, Kampala.
Methods: A quantitative, community-based analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among 383 women aged 15-49 years.

Data from 377 eligible participants were analysed using descriptive statistics and modified Poisson regression with robust standard errors to estimate adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
Results: Among 374 women with complete violence data, 72.5% (95% CI 67.7-76.7) reported at least one form of DGBV, while 49.7% experienced all four forms.
Emotional violence was most prevalent (65.2%), followed by physical (62.8%), sexual (59.9%) and economic violence (56.7%).
DGBV was not significantly associated with HIV testing or antenatal care attendance.
However, it was associated with current contraceptive use (aPR 1.11, 95% CI 1.01 -1.22) and partner interference with family planning (aPR 3.36, 95% CI: 1.25 -9.06).
Conclusion: DGBV was highly prevalent and frequently involved multiple forms of violence.
Despite high contraceptive use and antenatal care attendance, reproductive autonomy remained constrained by partner interference.
Integrating confidential, survivor-centred violence screening and reproductive autonomy support into SRH services is essential.
Domestic gender-based violence (DGBV), encompassing physical, sexual, emotional and economic violence within intimate relationships, is a major public health and human rights concern [1, 2].
text.formatted: Domestic gender-based violence (DGBV), encompassing physical, sexual, emotional and economic violence within intimate relationships, is a major public health and human rights concern <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>.

text.text: Data from the World Health Organization (WHO) suggests that approximately one in three women globally (nearly 840 million women aged 15 years and above) has experienced physical and/or sexual violence from intimate partners or non-partners in her lifetime, which has remained roughly constant over the last 20 years.

While physical and sexual abuse have historically garnered the most clinical and policy attention, abuse in the form of emotion control and economic control are likely to co-occur with physical violence and, together, render poly-victimisation-which may lead to enhanced mental health outcomes and reduced women's ability to earn a living from the household [2, 3].
text.formatted: While physical and sexual abuse have historically garnered the most clinical and policy attention, abuse in the form of emotion control and economic control are likely to co-occur with physical violence and, together, render poly-victimisation-which may lead to enhanced mental health outcomes and reduced women's ability to earn a living from the household <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3]</ref>.

text.text: In addition to the physical injuries, domestic gender-based violence (DGBV) has detrimental and long-term effects on women's sexual and reproductive health (SRH).
There is strong, consistent evidence that women experiencing DGBV are at increased risk of unwanted pregnancy, unsafe abortion, STIs, HIV and adverse pregnancy outcomes [4, 5].
text.formatted: There is strong, consistent evidence that women experiencing DGBV are at increased risk of unwanted pregnancy, unsafe abortion, STIs, HIV and adverse pregnancy outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5]</ref>.

text.text: DGBV may also be a structural and interpersonal barrier to accessing health care services.

Threatening partner behavior, fear of retribution, financial constraints and internalized stigma may diminish women's confidence to negotiate contraceptive use, to access appropriate ANC, to attend regular HIV testing sessions, or to obtain immediate treatment of STI symptoms [4] [5] [6].
text.formatted: Threatening partner behavior, fear of retribution, financial constraints and internalized stigma may diminish women's confidence to negotiate contraceptive use, to access appropriate ANC, to attend regular HIV testing sessions, or to obtain immediate treatment of STI symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[6]</ref>.

text.text: DGBV and negative sexual and reproductive health (SRH) outcomes are especially intertwined in Sub-Saharan Africa in settings where male supremacy, economic instability and infectious disease and endemic violence are prevalent [7].
text.formatted: DGBV and negative sexual and reproductive health (SRH) outcomes are especially intertwined in Sub-Saharan Africa in settings where male supremacy, economic instability and infectious disease and endemic violence are prevalent <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Meta-analyses at the regional level have demonstrated that lifetime prevalence of intimate partner violence in Sub-Saharan Africa is higher than the global estimate, at 36-44%, for ever partnered women.

Ugandan women continue to experience violence towards women in spite of progressive legal frameworks such as the Domestic Violence Act (2010) and the National Policy on Elimination of Gender-Based Violence [7, 8].
text.formatted: Ugandan women continue to experience violence towards women in spite of progressive legal frameworks such as the Domestic Violence Act (2010) and the National Policy on Elimination of Gender-Based Violence <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>.

text.text: In 2022, the Ugandan Demographic and Health Survey (UDHS) reported that 43.7% of all women (aged 15-49) ever in a union experienced physical violence and 16.7% (both physical and sexual violence combined) experienced sexual violence from their current or most recent intimate partner.

Prevalence of SRH service gaps such as high levels of unmet need for modern contraception, inadequate attendance to ANC, and postponement of STI/HIV services are likely leading to preventable maternal morbidity and transmission of HIV among women of reproductive age in Uganda [9, 10].
text.formatted: Prevalence of SRH service gaps such as high levels of unmet need for modern contraception, inadequate attendance to ANC, and postponement of STI/HIV services are likely leading to preventable maternal morbidity and transmission of HIV among women of reproductive age in Uganda <ref type="bibr">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr">10]</ref>.

text.text: In Uganda, the rapid growth of informal urban settlements lacking essential resources has increased community-level socioeconomic stresses that may influence both household violent interactions and access to SRH services for women and girls.

Among the high-density informal settlement residents of Lubaga Division of Kampala, where 78% of the population live in crowded single-room dwellings, informal daily wage labor, and with lack of personal financial independence, women are highly likely to be vulnerable to both household power dynamics and financial strife.

In a recent community-based study of suburban Kampala communities, the overall prevalence of violence against women was 53.3% indicating that the population is at substantial risk of both multidimensional domestic gender-based violence (DGBV) and limitations in access to SRH services due to compounded factors such as intense economic hardship, reliance on fee-paying private clinics, and dependence on male partners [10] [11] [12].
text.formatted: In a recent community-based study of suburban Kampala communities, the overall prevalence of violence against women was 53.3% indicating that the population is at substantial risk of both multidimensional domestic gender-based violence (DGBV) and limitations in access to SRH services due to compounded factors such as intense economic hardship, reliance on fee-paying private clinics, and dependence on male partners <ref type="bibr">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[12]</ref>.

text.text: However, despite the growing national acknowledgement of DGBV in Uganda, there remain notable evidence gaps at the micro-urban level.

Existing evidence provides limited community-level understanding of the co-occurrence of physical, sexual, emotional and economic violence and their relationship with women's sexual and reproductive health-seeking behaviour in informal urban settlements.

There is also limited community based quantitative evidence to determine if specific types and cumulative burdens of DGBV can lead to certain SRH-seeking behaviours, namely condom usage, STI treatment-seeking, HIV testing and antenatal care.

The following study has been designed to contribute to this gap by reporting: the prevalence of all types of DGBV; associated socio-demographic characteristics; and the relationship between exposure to each of these and all four types of SRH-seeking behaviour in a population of women living within the informal settlement of Lusaaze Zone, Lubaga Division, Kampala, Uganda.
We conducted a quantitative, community-based analytical cross-sectional study rooted in a postpositivist framework of objective measurement and statistical inference.
The study design involved the collection of data at one point in time to determine the prevalence and distribution of DGBV (descriptive study component).
The study further attempts to examine the relationship between DGBV, sociodemographic correlates, and SRH-seeking behavior (analytical study component).
Though this design is ideal for assessing burden of disease and violence, in this context where exposures and outcome are assessed at the same time, it was not able to establish causality.
This study was conducted in the Lusaaze Zone, Lubaga Division, Kampala District, Uganda.
Lusaaze was chosen because of the suspected domestic and gender-based violence and reproductive health challenges in this population that could be driven by the economic pressures of kampala.
The study population was women aged 15-49 years living in the Lusaaze Zone.
The target population was estimated at 900-1,300 women from local administrative estimates and community records.
The accessible population was women who had lived in Lusaaze for at least six months and who consented to take part (or assented with guardian consent, if aged under 18).
The sample population comprised all women in the age range of 15-49 years living in the Lusaaze Zone.

text.text: The calculated minimum sample size was 383 women.
A total of 383 women aged 15-49 years were enrolled in the study.
Participants were recruited using a systematic random sampling technique.

The sampling frame was compiled through a systematic enumeration of the residential households in the Lusaaze Zone with the assistance of local leaders and VHTs (Village Health Teams) resulting in 1,120 households identified as eligible for sampling from the Luzaase administrative register.
The sampling interval, k, was calculated using the formula: k = N/n (1,120/383 = 2.92).
The sampling interval was then rounded to three, k = 3.
A starting household was randomly generated, k = 1-3 using a random number generator, and one household was surveyed and sampled along the geographic axis.
The first household and subsequent homes were queried until reaching the sample size of 383 women.
Within each sampled household, one eligible woman between the ages of 15 and 49 was selected to participate.
If more than one woman was eligible, participants were selected via a simple random ballot method with numbered slips of paper folded and placed in a bowl.
If there was no eligible woman in a selected household, the next adjacent household was approached along the original geographic axis while not disturbing the original sampling frame.
If a respondent was unavailable at the time of survey, up to two repeated visits were conducted at different points in the day before moving on to the next household.
Using a structured instrument administered through interviews in either English or Luganda, as appropriate, data were obtained.

The questionnaire was administered face-to-face and in a private room by trained research assistants, which was likely to minimize researcher bias and potentially improve the accuracy of responses for persons with low literacy levels and to allow for clarification of sensitive questions.

The questionnaire covered three broad sections: (a) sociodemographic information, (b) domestic violence (i.e., physical, emotional, sexual, and economic violence) experiences and (c) sexual and reproductive healthseeking behaviors (i.e., antenatal care, family planning, HIV testing, and treatment-seeking for STI symptoms).
Data were captured on mobile data-collection forms or printed questionnaires, with audio recordings not utilized.
Data were collected via a structured interview.
The violence module asked specific questions about physical, sexual, emotional and economic violence.
The questions on sexual, emotional and economic violence specifically asked about violence by the respondent's current or most recent husband/partner and within the last 12 months.
Questions on physical violence did not specifically ask about who the violence was from or when it occurred.
Non-partner sexual violence was also asked about separately and was not included in the composite measure of DGBV.
Content validity was established through a detailed review by academic supervisors and other public health research experts.
Before the beginning of data collection, the pretested questionnaire in 20 women of a neighboring community with comparable sociodemographic settings, and the unclear issues were modified.
Also, the interviewers got training on conducting interviews, ethical issues, and assuring privacy of the respondents which is most likely to reduce respondent and interviewer bias.
Exposure: Domestic gender based violence was measured using four categories: physical, sexual, emotional and economic violence.
A positive answer to at least one question in each category indicated exposure to that type of violence.
Physical and sexual violence were indicated by any answer other than 'never'.
Emotional and economic violence were indicated by positive answers.
Sexual, emotional and economic violence questions asked about experiences with the respondents current or last husband/partner in the last 12 months.
Physical violence questions did not ask about the perpetrators or time frame.
Caution should be taken when interpreting this composite measure as there are differences in perpetrator and time frame between categories.
Non-partner sexual violence was also measured.

After adjustment, DGBV was not clearly associated with HIV testing or ANC attendance; current contraceptive use was modestly higher, and partner interference with family planning was more frequently reported among exposed ever-partnered women.

Partnership status showed the strongest association with the composite violence classification; however, this finding should be interpreted cautiously because three violence domains were measured specifically in relation to current or former partners.

This study identified a high prevalence of reported violence across four domains among women living in Lusaaze, Kampala.
However, differences in perpetrator attribution and recall periods across the questionnaire domains require caution when interpreting the composite estimate as domestic or intimate partner violence.
In general (72.5%) of the surveyed women who had completed the full battery of questions in each of the four DGBV questionnaires reported experiencing at least one form of DGBV.

The percentage of women reporting experience of DGBV was significantly higher than previous estimates from national surveys conducted in Uganda, such as Uganda's Demographic and Health Surveys, which estimated that thirty-five to fifty percent of ever married women experienced either physical or sexual violence during the year preceding the survey [15, 16].
text.formatted: The percentage of women reporting experience of DGBV was significantly higher than previous estimates from national surveys conducted in Uganda, such as Uganda's Demographic and Health Surveys, which estimated that thirty-five to fifty percent of ever married women experienced either physical or sexual violence during the year preceding the survey <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[15,</ref> <ref type="bibr">16]</ref>.

text.text: Nonetheless, these national survey estimates cannot be compared directly to those found in this study due to many methodological differences.

For example, national surveys employ stratified random samples from a large geographic area -commonly including rural areas while this study used systematic sampling of a small geographic area, a single peri-urban informal settlement.

Additionally, national surveys typically include items assessing physical and sexual violence only over a specific time period -e.g., past twelve month while this study included behavior-specific items assessing physical, sexual, emotional and economic violence.

The inclusion of behavioral items assessing emotional and economic violence may have contributed to increasing the number of cases detected in this study relative to studies that assess only physical and sexual violence.

Evidence exists suggesting that assessment tools focusing on both physical and sexual forms of violence underreport experiences of other types of violence when compared to assessment tools designed to measure all forms of violence [18, 19].
text.formatted: Evidence exists suggesting that assessment tools focusing on both physical and sexual forms of violence underreport experiences of other types of violence when compared to assessment tools designed to measure all forms of violence <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[18,</ref> <ref type="bibr">19]</ref>.

text.text: A further contributing factor to the high levels of reported DGBV in informal communities could be the presence of socioeconomic disadvantages and limited access to potential sources of support services.

While the current study did not collect sufficient data to determine whether these factors were causal determinants of the high rates of DGBV reported by women in this study [20, 21], they are likely to have been relevant factors.
text.formatted: While the current study did not collect sufficient data to determine whether these factors were causal determinants of the high rates of DGBV reported by women in this study <ref type="bibr">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr">21]</ref>, they are likely to have been relevant factors.

text.text: Emotional abuse was the most frequent type of violence reported at 65.2%.
The second highest frequency was for physical abuse at 62.8%, followed by sexual abuse at 59.9% and then economic abuse at 56.7%.
These rates are similar to other reports from sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia that report psychological abuse, either alone or with more than physical abuse.
In addition, nearly half (49.7%) of the sample were exposed to all four types of violence, suggesting that women in this sample were likely to experience a pattern of multiple exposures of violence.
When victims of violence experience two or more types of violence simultaneously it can be referred to as polyvictimization.
Polyvictimization is a serious issue since experiencing different forms of victimization can have additive negative impacts on mental and physical health [17, 24].
text.formatted: Polyvictimization is a serious issue since experiencing different forms of victimization can have additive negative impacts on mental and physical health <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">24]</ref>.

text.text: Of note, there were significantly greater percentages of currently partnered women (97.1%) who reported having experienced one or more forms of DGBV compared to previously partnered women (60.4%) and never partnered women (9.4%).

The higher prevalence of reported violence among currently partnered women highlights the importance of examining relationship context, while recognising that the study did not establish whether the current partner was responsible for every reported physical violence experience [25, 26].
text.formatted: The higher prevalence of reported violence among currently partnered women highlights the importance of examining relationship context, while recognising that the study did not establish whether the current partner was responsible for every reported physical violence experience <ref type="bibr">[25,</ref> <ref type="bibr">26]</ref>.

text.text: Although the rates of abuse among never partnered women are high, they should be interpreted cautiously.
There could be several explanations for these high rates, such as being abused by someone else in the same household or being abused in a previous relationship.
However, whether these abuses occurred in previous relationships will depend upon how the investigators define and measure abuse in the DGVB survey.

Abuse can occur against a woman by many people outside her intimate partner(s) whereas intimate partner violence refers only to violence from an individual's present or past intimate partner(s) [27, 28].
text.formatted: Abuse can occur against a woman by many people outside her intimate partner(s) whereas intimate partner violence refers only to violence from an individual's present or past intimate partner(s) <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">28]</ref>.

text.text: Understanding this difference is key to comparing our results with studies examining only partner specific violence, such as the Kenya DHS examination of intimate partner based sexual violence and the South African examination of physical violence by present or past partner(s) [25, 29].

text.text: There was not a consistent relationship found between DGBV and utilization of SRH services.
As indicated earlier, we did find a statistically non-significant association between DGBV and use of HIV testing (aPR 0.99, 95% CI: 0.82 -1.20).

Our finding contradicts those from an intervention trial in Nairobi, Kenya where screening for intimate partner violence during HIV counseling resulted in increased self-reporting of both HIV testing and use of HIV related services [30].
text.formatted: Our finding contradicts those from an intervention trial in Nairobi, Kenya where screening for intimate partner violence during HIV counseling resulted in increased self-reporting of both HIV testing and use of HIV related services <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[30]</ref>.

text.text: However, the studies differ substantially in design and setting: the Nairobi study evaluated an intervention among clinic attendees, whereas the present study examined community-level associations.
Furthermore, HIV testing coverage in Lusaaze was already high (84.3%), potentially limiting the observable variation needed to identify differences between exposure groups.

Violence may also influence testing in opposing directions: fear of partner retaliation may discourage testing, while perceived HIV risk or the need for reproductive health information may motivate it [31] [32] [33].
text.formatted: Violence may also influence testing in opposing directions: fear of partner retaliation may discourage testing, while perceived HIV risk or the need for reproductive health information may motivate it <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[31]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[32]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[33]</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the absence of an association should not be interpreted as evidence that violence has no influence on HIV testing decisions.
DGBV was not significantly associated with ANC attendance (aPR 0.93, 95% CI: 0.84-1.02).
This contrasts with evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses that intimate partner violence is associated with reduced adequate utilisation of ANC services [34, 35].
text.formatted: This contrasts with evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses that intimate partner violence is associated with reduced adequate utilisation of ANC services <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[34,</ref> <ref type="bibr">35]</ref>.

text.text: However, the near universal attendance of every pregnant woman (98.4%) may explain why this association was not significant due to limited variation.

Evidence from a 36 country analysis of DHS data suggests that lifetime intimate partner violence is more consistently associated with reduced completion of recommended ANC visits and delivery at a facility [36].
text.formatted: Evidence from a 36 country analysis of DHS data suggests that lifetime intimate partner violence is more consistently associated with reduced completion of recommended ANC visits and delivery at a facility <ref type="bibr">[36]</ref>.

text.text: However, the measure of whether women attended ANC at least once may not capture the full picture of how intimate partner violence impacts on women's ANC.
In high initial contact settings, intimate partner violence may impact on women's ability to adequately access and utilise services [36].
text.formatted: In high initial contact settings, intimate partner violence may impact on women's ability to adequately access and utilise services <ref type="bibr">[36]</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, the high ANC attendance in Lusaaze should not be taken to mean that women are accessing equitable and violence free maternal health services.
A notable finding was the modest positive association between DGBV and current contraceptive use (aPR 1.11, 95% CI: 1.01-1.22).
This is contrary to findings showing that women exposed to intimate partner violence have reduced contraceptive use [23, 37].
text.formatted: This is contrary to findings showing that women exposed to intimate partner violence have reduced contraceptive use <ref type="bibr">[23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">37]</ref>.

text.text: However, this is consistent with findings from Bawuah et al (38) who found that women experiencing intimate partner violence had higher modern contraceptive use but lower adequate maternal health utilisation from a 25 country DHS analysis in Africa.
text.formatted: However, this is consistent with findings from Bawuah et al <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(38)</ref> who found that women experiencing intimate partner violence had higher modern contraceptive use but lower adequate maternal health utilisation from a 25 country DHS analysis in Africa.

text.text: This suggests that contraceptive use and maternal health utilisation may be impacted in opposing ways by relationship control.
One possible explanation for this is that women are using contraceptives discreetly.
Studies from Uganda and Bangladesh have shown that women are using discreet contraceptive methods to retain some control over their reproduction within controlling or abusive relationships [39, 40].
text.formatted: Studies from Uganda and Bangladesh have shown that women are using discreet contraceptive methods to retain some control over their reproduction within controlling or abusive relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">[39,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">40]</ref>.

text.text: This could therefore explain the association seen in Lusaaze.
Another factor to consider is whether the association is due to reverse causation.
Women using contraception may cause suspicion from their partner.
Longitudinal and qualitative studies are needed to determine if women are making autonomous decisions around contraceptive use or if they are using discreet contraceptive methods.
It should be noted that only 14 women were non-users so this may have impacted on the stability of the results [44].
text.formatted: It should be noted that only 14 women were non-users so this may have impacted on the stability of the results <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">[44]</ref>.

text.text: The strongest association with an SRH outcome was partner interference with family planning (aPR 3.36, 95% CI: 1.25-9.06).
Nearly half of ever partnered women (48.2%) experienced interference with family planning.
Women who experienced DGBV had over 3 times higher prevalence of partner interference.
This suggests that reproductive coercion is an important aspect of violence experienced in Lusaaze.

The reproductive coercion framework explains how women experience sabotage of contraceptive use, pressure to conceive and interference with contraceptive decision making from their partner which limits their reproductive autonomy [41, 45].
text.formatted: The reproductive coercion framework explains how women experience sabotage of contraceptive use, pressure to conceive and interference with contraceptive decision making from their partner which limits their reproductive autonomy <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[41,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">45]</ref>.

text.text: This is consistent with qualitative findings from Wakiso District in Uganda where women reported that their partners would break contraceptive pills, refuse to use condoms and pressure them to conceive [39].
text.formatted: This is consistent with qualitative findings from Wakiso District in Uganda where women reported that their partners would break contraceptive pills, refuse to use condoms and pressure them to conceive <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">[39]</ref>.

text.text: Similar findings have been seen in Bangladesh and India where women have reported partner and family resistance including in-laws to contraceptive use [40, 37].
text.formatted: Similar findings have been seen in Bangladesh and India where women have reported partner and family resistance including in-laws to contraceptive use <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">[40,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">37]</ref>.

text.text: However, the wide confidence interval suggests that there is a lot of uncertainty around the strength of this association.
There were only a small number of ever partnered women who were not exposed (n=18).
This is an issue with sparse data and can be particularly problematic in areas where prevalence is high.
This reduces the stability of the adjusted estimates [46, 47].

text.text: The sociodemographic findings show that DGBV is influenced by a range of individual and relationship factors.
Women with no or primary education (aPR 1.13) and secondary education (aPR 1.12) had higher prevalence of DGBV compared to those with tertiary education.
This is generally consistent with evidence showing women with lower levels of education are more vulnerable to intimate partner violence [48, 49].
text.formatted: This is generally consistent with evidence showing women with lower levels of education are more vulnerable to intimate partner violence <ref type="bibr">[48,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">49]</ref>.

text.text: However, there was not a large difference so it cannot be said that women with tertiary education are protected from DGBV.
Education may be an indicator of wider socioeconomic differences, economic opportunities and power in relationships.
It may also influence whether women are able to identify, report and leave abusive relationships [50, 51].
text.formatted: It may also influence whether women are able to identify, report and leave abusive relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">[50,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">51]</ref>.

text.text: Women who were self-employed had higher prevalence of DGBV (aPR 1.08).
Whilst this may increase women's financial independence it does not necessarily increase their power in relationships.
Women may challenge traditional gender norms by becoming economically active which can cause conflict and violence [52, 53].
text.formatted: Women may challenge traditional gender norms by becoming economically active which can cause conflict and violence <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">[52,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">53]</ref>.

text.text: This shows the importance of understanding violence beyond just individual socioeconomic factors and considering how gendered power and resources are distributed [54, 55].
text.formatted: This shows the importance of understanding violence beyond just individual socioeconomic factors and considering how gendered power and resources are distributed <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">[54,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">55]</ref>.

text.text: Age was not significantly associated with DGBV.
This is contrary to studies showing that younger women are more likely to experience violence [56, 57].
text.formatted: This is contrary to studies showing that younger women are more likely to experience violence <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">[56,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">57]</ref>.

text.text: However, this is not necessarily conflicting as there is evidence that women experience violence throughout their reproductive life.
This may also be due to the high proportion of women aged between 35-49 years old (45.4%).
There may also be differences in relationship transitions such as separation and widowhood.
The findings regarding STI symptoms should be treated with caution.
The high prevalence of symptoms (94.4%) and seeking treatment (94.1%) may not be accurate due to issues with how symptoms were categorised.
Symptoms such as discharge and itch are not specific to STIs and could be caused by other gynaecological or physiological issues.
This has been seen in other studies using symptoms as a method of screening [59,60].

Therefore, it cannot be confidently said that there is no association between DGBV and seeking treatment for STIs as the outcome may not accurately reflect true STI morbidity or appropriate treatment.
Future studies should include lab confirmed STI testing or validated syndromic algorithms with clear time frames [18].
text.formatted: Future studies should include lab confirmed STI testing or validated syndromic algorithms with clear time frames <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[18]</ref>.

text.text: Overall, the findings can be best understood using the social ecological model, feminist perspectives and reproductive coercion.
The social ecological model considers that violence occurs due to a combination of individual, relationship and community factors.
Feminist perspectives consider power imbalances in relationships to control women's bodies and reproduction [55, 54, 61].
text.formatted: Feminist perspectives consider power imbalances in relationships to control women's bodies and reproduction <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">[55,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">54,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">61]</ref>.

text.text: Reproductive coercion explains how women's reproduction is controlled by their partner through interfering with contraceptive use and conception decisions [41, 45].
text.formatted: Reproductive coercion explains how women's reproduction is controlled by their partner through interfering with contraceptive use and conception decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[41,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">45]</ref>.

text.text: The high prevalence of contraceptive use combined with high partner interference shows that traditional measures of service use may not fully reflect women's reproductive autonomy.
Women may be accessing contraception but still experience limited control over their reproduction.
This demonstrates that women may not be empowered, making informed decisions or free from coercion [39, 40, 62].
text.formatted: This demonstrates that women may not be empowered, making informed decisions or free from coercion <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">[39,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">40,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">62]</ref>.

text.text: This should be interpreted with consideration to the limitations.
The study was cross-sectional meaning that it is not possible to determine causation or temporality.
There was also no clear time frame for violence meaning that the results may not be as accurate.
Non-response may have caused bias.
There were issues with the validity of the STI questions and the exact measure of violence.
There were a limited number of currently partnered women who were not exposed meaning some of the adjusted estimates were not as accurate.
Particularly the association between partner interference with family planning.
However, the study provides evidence from a community setting in an under-researched informal urban area.
It looked at a range of different types of violence and included specific behaviours.
The decisions made during analysis were reported meaning the findings are transparent.

From a public health perspective, interventions should go beyond increasing women's service use and consider improving safety, confidentiality, reproductive autonomy and identifying partner interference.
Women may not be empowered as they have high ANC attendance and contraceptive uptake but relationship coercion is still prevalent [36, 63].
text.formatted: Women may not be empowered as they have high ANC attendance and contraceptive uptake but relationship coercion is still prevalent <ref type="bibr">[36,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">63]</ref>.

text.text: There were different ways of asking about perpetrators of violence.
The questions on sexual, emotional and economic violence specifically asked about current or ex-husbands/partners in the last 12 months.
Questions on physical violence were not specific about perpetrators or time frame.
This means the 4 domain composite combines different time frames and cannot be viewed as a single measure of intimate partner violence in the last year.
Future studies should be longitudinal and include validated reproductive coercion measures.
Lab confirmed STI testing should also be included.
The quality, continuity and autonomy of care should also be considered.
This would provide better evidence to implement integrated gender sensitive interventions to improve women's SRH in informal urban settlements.
Violence exposure across multiple domains was common among women in Lusaaze.
The coexistence of contraceptive use and partner interference with family planning highlights the limitations of healthcare utilisation as a standalone indicator of reproductive autonomy.
Survivor-centred SRH services should address violence, confidentiality and reproductive decision-making.
SRH services should offer confidential, survivor focussed strategies to identify violence and reproductive coercion in informal urban settings.
There should be clear referral routes for psychosocial, legal and protection services.
Confidentiality should be maintained whilst supporting women to make their own decisions on contraception.
Public health strategies should also be implemented to reduce violence in the community.
Longitudinal and mixed methods studies should be conducted to understand the causal pathways.
Validated tools should be used to measure violence and reproductive coercion.

The study received ethics approval from the Uganda Heart Institute Research Ethics Committee (REC: UHIREC0192) with institutional clearance by Victoria University and administrative permission from the Lusaaze Zone Local Chairperson in Lubaga Division, Kampala.
The researcher adhered to the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki which include respect for persons, voluntary participation, anonymity and confidentiality, beneficence and justice.

Written informed consent was obtained from adult participants before conducting interviews; written informed assent was obtained from 15-17 year olds in conjunction with written informed consent from their parents or guardians.

Participants were appropriately informed of the purpose of the study, its risks and benefits, and that their participation was voluntary and they could refuse or withdraw at any time, without penalty.
Interviews were conducted in private to ensure privacy and confidentiality, names were not recorded and participants were given identifiers on each record.
Participants experiencing distress were treated with dignity and referred to local health and psychosocial services.
Data was stored securely in password protected files and filing cabinets for use in the research and academic work.
